q: You need to ensure that an EC2 instance retains its public IP address even after being stopped and started. Which feature should you use?

exp.a: Incorrect – Auto-assigned public IPs change when an instance is stopped and started.
exp.b: Correct – Elastic IP provides a static public IPv4 address that persists across stop/start cycles.
exp.c: Incorrect – Private IPs are internal and not accessible from the internet.
exp.d: Incorrect – IPv6 addresses are persistent but this is not the standard solution for retaining a public IPv4.

q: An application requires consistent low-latency performance and guaranteed IOPS. Which EBS volume type should you choose?

exp.a: Incorrect – gp2 IOPS scale with volume size and may not guarantee consistent performance.
exp.b: Incorrect – gp3 provides up to 16,000 IOPS but io2 provides higher guaranteed IOPS.
exp.c: Correct – io2 (Provisioned IOPS SSD) provides consistent, guaranteed IOPS up to 64,000 (or 256,000 with Block Express).
exp.d: Incorrect – st1 is throughput-optimized HDD, not suitable for low-latency IOPS workloads.

q: What is the maximum ratio of provisioned IOPS to volume size (in GiB) for io1/io2 EBS volumes?

exp.a: Incorrect – The ratio for io1 is 50:1, not 10:1.
exp.b: Incorrect – 50:1 is the ratio for io1. io2 supports 500:1.
exp.c: Correct – io2 volumes support up to 500 IOPS per GiB of volume size.
exp.d: Incorrect – 1000:1 exceeds the maximum ratio.

q: Which scaling policy type in Auto Scaling adjusts capacity based on a target value for a specific CloudWatch metric?

exp.a: Incorrect – Simple Scaling adds/removes a fixed number of instances based on a single alarm.
exp.b: Incorrect – Step Scaling adjusts capacity in steps based on alarm severity.
exp.c: Correct – Target Tracking Scaling automatically adjusts capacity to maintain a target value (e.g., CPU at 50%).
exp.d: Incorrect – Scheduled Scaling scales based on time/date, not a metric value.

q: You want your Auto Scaling Group to scale out when CPU utilization exceeds 70%. Which type of scaling policy should you configure?

exp.a: Incorrect – Scheduled Scaling is time-based, not metric-based.
exp.b: Incorrect – Predictive Scaling uses ML to forecast, not react to current CPU.
exp.c: Correct – Target Tracking Scaling can be set to maintain average CPU utilization at a target (e.g., 70%), scaling in/out automatically.
exp.d: Incorrect – Manual Scaling requires human intervention.

q: What is the maximum number of security groups you can assign to a single EC2 instance (network interface)?

exp.a: Incorrect – The default limit is 5.
exp.b: Correct – By default, you can assign up to 5 security groups per network interface.
exp.c: Incorrect – 10 exceeds the default.
exp.d: Incorrect – 16 exceeds the default.

q: What is the default maximum number of rules per security group?

exp.a: Incorrect – The default is 60 inbound and 60 outbound rules.
exp.b: Incorrect – The limit is 60, not 50.
exp.c: Correct – Each security group allows up to 60 inbound rules and 60 outbound rules by default.
exp.d: Incorrect – 100 exceeds the default limit.

q: A company needs to run a workload that can tolerate interruptions and wants maximum cost savings. Which purchasing option is best?

exp.a: Incorrect – On-Demand provides no discount.
exp.b: Incorrect – Reserved Instances require commitment and provide less discount than Spot.
exp.c: Correct – Spot Instances offer up to 90% discount and are ideal for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads.
exp.d: Incorrect – Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive option.

q: Which Spot Instance request type allows you to define the maximum number of instances, target capacity, and instance pools?

exp.a: Incorrect – Spot Blocks reserve instances for a defined duration (1-6 hours) but are now deprecated.
exp.b: Correct – Spot Fleet allows you to request a fleet of Spot (and optionally On-Demand) instances, defining capacity targets across multiple pools.
exp.c: Incorrect – One-time requests are simple single-instance requests.
exp.d: Incorrect – Persistent requests relaunch if interrupted but don't define fleets.

q: Which feature of EBS allows you to increase volume size, change volume type, or adjust IOPS without detaching the volume?

exp.a: Incorrect – Snapshots are for backup, not for live modifications.
exp.b: Correct – EBS Elastic Volumes allows you to dynamically modify volume size, type, and IOPS while the volume is attached.
exp.c: Incorrect – Multi-Attach allows multiple instances to share a volume.
exp.d: Incorrect – Encryption secures data, it doesn't modify volume properties.

q: You have an EBS volume in us-east-1a and need to use it in us-east-1b. What should you do?

opts.a: Detach and attach directly to an instance in us-east-1b
opts.b: Create a snapshot and then create a new volume in us-east-1b from the snapshot
opts.d: Copy the volume directly using AWS CLI

exp.a: Incorrect – EBS volumes are AZ-specific and cannot be moved directly between AZs.
exp.b: Correct – You must create a snapshot of the volume, then create a new volume from that snapshot in the desired AZ.
exp.c: Incorrect – Multi-Attach works within the same AZ only.
exp.d: Incorrect – There is no direct volume copy command between AZs.

q: Which EBS volume type is best suited for big data and data warehouse workloads requiring high throughput?

exp.a: Incorrect – gp3 is general purpose SSD, not optimized for sequential throughput.
exp.b: Incorrect – io2 is for high IOPS workloads, not specifically throughput.
exp.c: Correct – st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) provides up to 500 MiB/s throughput, ideal for big data and log processing.
exp.d: Incorrect – sc1 is Cold HDD for infrequent access with lower throughput.

q: What is the maximum throughput for an st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) EBS volume?

exp.a: Incorrect – 250 MiB/s is the max for sc1.
exp.b: Correct – st1 supports a maximum throughput of 500 MiB/s.
exp.c: Incorrect – 750 MiB/s exceeds st1 limits.
exp.d: Incorrect – 1,000 MiB/s exceeds st1 limits.

q: Which of the following EBS volume types CANNOT be used as a boot volume?

exp.a: Incorrect – gp2 can be used as a boot volume.
exp.b: Incorrect – gp3 can be used as a boot volume.
exp.c: Incorrect – io2 can be used as a boot volume.
exp.d: Correct – st1 (HDD) and sc1 (HDD) cannot be used as boot volumes. Only SSD types (gp2, gp3, io1, io2) can be boot volumes.

q: How does EBS encryption work regarding snapshots?

opts.b: Encrypted volumes produce encrypted snapshots automatically
opts.c: You must manually encrypt each snapshot

exp.a: Incorrect – Snapshots from encrypted volumes are always encrypted.
exp.b: Correct – If the source EBS volume is encrypted, all snapshots created from it are automatically encrypted.
exp.c: Incorrect – Encryption is automatic for snapshots of encrypted volumes.
exp.d: Incorrect – Snapshots can be encrypted.

q: How can you encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume?

opts.a: Enable encryption on the existing volume directly
opts.b: Create a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, then create a new volume from the encrypted snapshot
opts.c: Use AWS KMS to encrypt in-place
opts.d: Detach the volume and it will auto-encrypt

exp.a: Incorrect – You cannot enable encryption on an existing unencrypted volume directly.
exp.b: Correct – The process is: snapshot → copy snapshot with encryption → create encrypted volume from copied snapshot.
exp.c: Incorrect – KMS provides the keys but doesn't encrypt volumes in-place.
exp.d: Incorrect – Detaching does not trigger encryption.

q: What is the purpose of the DeleteOnTermination attribute for an EBS volume?

opts.a: Determines if the volume is deleted when detached
opts.b: Determines if the volume is deleted when the attached EC2 instance is terminated
opts.d: Determines if the instance is terminated when volume is deleted

exp.a: Incorrect – This attribute relates to instance termination, not detachment.
exp.b: Correct – DeleteOnTermination controls whether the EBS volume is automatically deleted when the EC2 instance it's attached to is terminated.
exp.c: Incorrect – This attribute does not affect snapshots.
exp.d: Incorrect – It's about the volume being deleted, not the instance.

q: By default, what is the DeleteOnTermination setting for the root EBS volume?

exp.a: Incorrect – The root volume is deleted by default on termination.
exp.b: Correct – The root EBS volume has DeleteOnTermination set to true by default. Additional volumes default to false.
exp.c: Incorrect – It does not depend on instance type.
exp.d: Incorrect – It does not depend on volume type.

q: Which EC2 Placement Group strategy is best for applications that need low network latency and high throughput between instances?

exp.a: Incorrect – Spread distributes instances across hardware for high availability.
exp.b: Correct – Cluster placement group packs instances close together within a single AZ for low-latency, high-throughput networking.
exp.c: Incorrect – Partition spreads instances across logical partitions.
exp.d: Incorrect – Default is not a placement group strategy.

q: Which placement group strategy is commonly used for large distributed and replicated workloads like HDFS, HBase, and Cassandra?

exp.a: Incorrect – Cluster is for low-latency within a single AZ, not distributed workloads.
exp.b: Incorrect – Spread limits to 7 instances per AZ, too few for large workloads.
exp.c: Correct – Partition placement groups divide instances into partitions on separate racks, ideal for distributed big data workloads.
exp.d: Incorrect – Dedicated is not a placement group type.

q: What is the maximum number of partitions per Availability Zone in a Partition Placement Group?

exp.a: Incorrect – The maximum is 7.
exp.b: Incorrect – The maximum is 7.
exp.c: Correct – You can have up to 7 partitions per AZ in a Partition Placement Group.
exp.d: Incorrect – 10 exceeds the limit.

q: Which type of Load Balancer provides a static IP address per AZ?

exp.a: Incorrect – ALB does not provide a static IP; it uses DNS names.
exp.b: Correct – Network Load Balancer provides a static IP per AZ and also supports Elastic IP assignment.
exp.c: Incorrect – CLB does not provide static IPs.
exp.d: Incorrect – Gateway Load Balancer does not provide static IPs to clients.

q: What is the purpose of a Target Group in the context of an ALB?

opts.a: To define which ports to open on the firewall
opts.b: To group EC2 instances (or other targets) that receive traffic from the load balancer

exp.a: Incorrect – Firewalls are managed by Security Groups/NACLs.
exp.b: Correct – Target Groups define a set of targets (EC2, Lambda, IP addresses, etc.) that the ALB routes traffic to based on listener rules.
exp.c: Incorrect – DNS records are managed by Route 53.
exp.d: Incorrect – Auto Scaling policies are separate from Target Groups.

q: Which health check types are available for instances in an Auto Scaling Group?

exp.a: Incorrect – ASG supports both EC2 and ELB health checks.
exp.b: Incorrect – ELB health checks can be added but EC2 health checks are also available.
exp.c: Correct – Auto Scaling Groups support EC2 status checks (default) and ELB health checks (when attached to a load balancer).
exp.d: Incorrect – CloudWatch alarms can trigger scaling but are not a health check type for ASG.

q: What is the default health check grace period for an Auto Scaling Group?

exp.a: Incorrect – 60 seconds is too short.
exp.b: Incorrect – 120 seconds is not the default.
exp.c: Correct – The default health check grace period is 300 seconds, allowing instances time to boot before being checked.
exp.d: Incorrect – 600 seconds is not the default.

q: Which Auto Scaling termination policy is used by default?

opts.c: Default (AZ balance → oldest launch configuration → closest to billing hour)

exp.a: Incorrect – Oldest Instance is a configurable policy but not the default.
exp.b: Incorrect – Newest Instance is not the default.
exp.c: Correct – The default termination policy first balances AZs, then selects instances with the oldest launch configuration, then closest to billing hour.
exp.d: Incorrect – Random is not the default.

q: What is Connection Draining (or Deregistration Delay) in ELB?

opts.a: Time allowed for unhealthy instances to recover
opts.b: Time allowed to complete in-flight requests before deregistering an instance
opts.c: Time to establish a new connection

exp.a: Incorrect – This describes a health check grace period.
exp.b: Correct – Connection Draining (Deregistration Delay) gives in-flight requests time to complete before the instance is removed from the target group. Default is 300 seconds.
exp.c: Incorrect – Connection establishment time is not Connection Draining.
exp.d: Incorrect – Idle timeout is a different setting.

q: What is the default deregistration delay (connection draining) timeout for an ELB target group?

exp.a: Incorrect – 30 seconds is not the default.
exp.b: Incorrect – 60 seconds is not the default.
exp.c: Correct – The default deregistration delay is 300 seconds (5 minutes).
exp.d: Incorrect – 600 seconds is not the default.

q: Which ALB feature allows you to route requests to the same target based on cookies?

exp.a: Incorrect – Path-based routing directs traffic based on URL path.
exp.b: Incorrect – Host-based routing directs based on hostname.
exp.c: Correct – Sticky Sessions use cookies to ensure a user's requests are routed to the same target for the session duration.
exp.d: Incorrect – Cross-zone load balancing distributes traffic evenly across all AZs.

q: What is Cross-Zone Load Balancing?

opts.a: Load balancing across different AWS regions
opts.b: Distributing traffic evenly across all registered instances in all enabled AZs
opts.c: Routing traffic only within the same AZ
opts.d: Balancing between public and private subnets

exp.a: Incorrect – Cross-zone is across AZs within a region, not across regions.
exp.b: Correct – Cross-Zone Load Balancing distributes traffic evenly across all registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones.
exp.c: Incorrect – Without cross-zone, traffic stays within the same AZ.
exp.d: Incorrect – It's about AZ distribution, not subnet types.

q: Is Cross-Zone Load Balancing enabled by default for ALB?

opts.a: Yes, enabled by default and free

exp.a: Correct – For ALB, cross-zone load balancing is enabled by default at no additional charge.
exp.b: Incorrect – It is enabled by default for ALB (NLB requires manual enabling and charges apply).
exp.c: Incorrect – No additional charges for ALB cross-zone.
exp.d: Incorrect – ALB supports cross-zone load balancing.

q: Which EC2 feature allows you to use software licenses that are bound to physical hardware (e.g., per-socket, per-core)?

exp.a: Incorrect – Reserved Instances don't give you visibility into physical hardware.
exp.b: Correct – Dedicated Hosts provide visibility into sockets and physical cores, allowing you to use existing server-bound licenses (BYOL).
exp.c: Incorrect – Spot Instances run on shared hardware.
exp.d: Incorrect – Placement Groups control placement but don't provide hardware-level licensing info.

q: What is an EC2 Capacity Reservation?

opts.a: A discounted instance like Reserved Instances
opts.b: A reservation of compute capacity in a specific AZ regardless of usage

exp.a: Incorrect – Capacity Reservations ensure capacity but do not provide billing discounts by themselves.
exp.b: Correct – EC2 Capacity Reservations reserve capacity in a specific AZ, ensuring you can launch instances when needed. No discount unless combined with Savings Plans/RIs.
exp.c: Incorrect – Spot Instances have no reservation queue.
exp.d: Incorrect – It's not related to placement groups.

q: What is the difference between Convertible and Standard Reserved Instances?

opts.a: Convertible RIs can change instance family, OS, and tenancy; Standard cannot
opts.b: Standard RIs are cheaper but Convertible RIs last longer
opts.d: Standard RIs can only be used in one AZ

exp.a: Correct – Convertible RIs allow you to change instance family, OS, scope, and tenancy. Standard RIs offer higher discount (~72%) but are less flexible.
exp.b: Incorrect – Both have 1 or 3-year terms.
exp.c: Incorrect – They differ in flexibility and discount levels.
exp.d: Incorrect – Both Regional and Zonal scopes are available for Standard RIs.

q: What is the maximum discount offered by Convertible Reserved Instances?

exp.a: Incorrect – Convertible RIs offer more than 36%.
exp.b: Incorrect – The maximum is approximately 66%.
exp.c: Correct – Convertible Reserved Instances offer up to approximately 66% discount (compared to 72% for Standard RIs).
exp.d: Incorrect – 72% is the maximum for Standard Reserved Instances.

q: What is the Savings Plans alternative to Reserved Instances that offers flexibility across instance families?

exp.a: Correct – Compute Savings Plans offer up to 66% discount and provide flexibility across instance families, regions, OS, and tenancy. They also apply to Fargate and Lambda.
exp.b: Incorrect – EC2 Instance Savings Plans are locked to a specific instance family in a region (up to 72% off).
exp.c: Incorrect – Storage Savings Plans do not exist.
exp.d: Incorrect – Network Savings Plans do not exist.

q: Which lifecycle hook stages are available in an Auto Scaling Group?

exp.a: Correct – Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks put instances in Pending:Wait (during launch) or Terminating:Wait (during termination) states.
exp.b: Incorrect – These are not valid lifecycle hook states.
exp.c: Incorrect – These are not the correct state names.
exp.d: Incorrect – These are not valid states.

q: What is the maximum duration an instance can remain in a lifecycle hook wait state?

exp.a: Incorrect – The default is 1 hour but maximum is 48 hours.
exp.b: Incorrect – 2 hours is not the maximum.
exp.c: Incorrect – 24 hours is not the maximum.
exp.d: Correct – The maximum wait time for a lifecycle hook is 48 hours (or 100 times the heartbeat timeout, whichever is smaller).

q: Which AWS service can be used with EC2 to run containers without managing the underlying infrastructure?

exp.a: Correct – AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers (ECS/EKS) that eliminates the need to manage EC2 instances.
exp.b: Incorrect – Lambda runs functions, not containers.
exp.c: Incorrect – AWS Batch can use EC2 or Fargate but is for batch processing jobs.
exp.d: Incorrect – Step Functions orchestrate workflows, not containers.

q: What happens when you reboot an EC2 instance?

opts.a: The public IP changes and instance store data is lost
opts.b: The public IP remains the same and instance store data is preserved
opts.c: The instance moves to a new host

exp.a: Incorrect – Rebooting does not change the public IP or lose instance store data.
exp.b: Correct – A reboot keeps the instance on the same host, preserving the public IP, private IP, instance store data, and EBS attachments.
exp.c: Incorrect – Reboot does not migrate the instance.
exp.d: Incorrect – EBS volumes remain attached.

q: Which EC2 instance metadata category provides the IAM role credentials for the instance?

exp.a: Incorrect – This returns the AMI ID.
exp.b: Correct – IAM role temporary credentials are available at /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name>.
exp.c: Incorrect – This returns the user data script.
exp.d: Incorrect – This returns SSH public keys.

q: What is IMDSv2 and why is it recommended?

opts.a: Version 2 of the Instance Metadata Service that requires session-based tokens for security

exp.a: Correct – IMDSv2 uses session-oriented requests with a token (PUT then GET), protecting against SSRF attacks.
exp.b: Incorrect – IMDS is the metadata service, not an instance type.
exp.c: Incorrect – IMDS is unrelated to EBS.
exp.d: Incorrect – IMDS is an EC2 feature, not a VPC feature.

q: Which AWS service allows you to automate the creation of AMIs on a schedule?

exp.a: Incorrect – AWS Backup handles backup plans for various services but EC2 Image Builder specifically builds/tests/distributes AMIs.
exp.b: Correct – EC2 Image Builder automates the creation, testing, and distribution of AMIs and container images on a schedule.
exp.c: Incorrect – CloudFormation is for infrastructure as code, not AMI building.
exp.d: Incorrect – Data Lifecycle Manager automates EBS snapshot lifecycle, not AMI creation.

q: What is Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) used for?

opts.b: Automating the creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots

exp.a: Incorrect – S3 lifecycle policies handle S3 objects.
exp.b: Correct – DLM automates EBS snapshot creation, retention, and deletion based on policies.
exp.c: Incorrect – Auto Scaling manages instance lifecycles.
exp.d: Incorrect – IAM handles key rotation.

q: What is the purpose of an EC2 Status Check?

opts.b: To monitor the health of the instance and underlying hardware

exp.a: Incorrect – Status Checks are not related to billing.
exp.b: Correct – EC2 Status Checks include System Status Check (AWS hardware/network issues) and Instance Status Check (software/OS issues).
exp.c: Incorrect – IAM permissions are separate.
exp.d: Incorrect – Bandwidth is monitored via CloudWatch metrics.

q: If a System Status Check fails on your EC2 instance, what is the recommended action?

opts.b: Stop and start the instance (to migrate to new hardware)

exp.a: Incorrect – Rebooting keeps the instance on the same hardware; system issues are host-level.
exp.b: Correct – Stopping and starting migrates the instance to a new physical host, resolving hardware-related system status check failures.
exp.c: Incorrect – Termination is unnecessary; stop/start is sufficient.
exp.d: Incorrect – While you can contact support, stop/start is the immediate fix.

q: What is Enhanced Networking on EC2?

opts.a: A feature that adds a firewall to the instance
opts.b: A feature that provides higher bandwidth, lower latency, and lower jitter using SR-IOV
opts.d: A paid add-on for network monitoring

exp.a: Incorrect – Firewalls are managed by Security Groups.
exp.b: Correct – Enhanced Networking uses SR-IOV (Single Root I/O Virtualization) to provide higher PPS (packets per second), lower latency, and lower jitter at no extra cost.
exp.c: Incorrect – IPv6 is separate from Enhanced Networking.
exp.d: Incorrect – Enhanced Networking is available at no additional cost on supported instances.

q: What is the maximum network bandwidth available on EC2 instances with ENA (Elastic Network Adapter)?

exp.a: Incorrect – Many instance types support more than 10 Gbps.
exp.b: Incorrect – Some instances support up to 100 Gbps.
exp.c: Correct – With ENA, certain instance types (like C5n, P4d) support up to 100 Gbps network bandwidth.
exp.d: Incorrect – 400 Gbps is for EFA (Elastic Fabric Adapter) with specific HPC instances, but standard ENA maxes at 100 Gbps.

q: What is the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA)?

opts.b: A network interface for high-performance computing (HPC) with OS-bypass capabilities

exp.a: Incorrect – EFA is a network interface, not a storage interface.
exp.b: Correct – EFA is a network device for EC2 that provides high-throughput, low-latency networking with OS-bypass for HPC and ML workloads.
exp.c: Incorrect – EFA is not a load balancer.
exp.d: Incorrect – EFA is not a monitoring agent.

q: Which EC2 Nitro feature provides hardware-based security for encryption keys?

exp.a: Correct – Nitro Enclaves provide isolated compute environments for processing highly sensitive data like encryption keys, PII.
exp.b: Incorrect – Nitro Security Chip protects the hardware and firmware but doesn't provide application-level enclaves.
exp.c: Incorrect – Nitro Cards offload I/O functions.
exp.d: Incorrect – Nitro Hypervisor is lightweight but doesn't provide isolated enclaves.

q: What is the maximum number of ENIs (Elastic Network Interfaces) you can attach to an EC2 instance?

opts.a: It depends on the instance type

exp.a: Correct – The number of ENIs you can attach depends on the instance type. For example, m5.large supports 3, while m5.24xlarge supports 15.
exp.b: Incorrect – The limit varies by instance type.
exp.c: Incorrect – The limit varies.
exp.d: Incorrect – There is always a limit based on instance type.

q: You need to run a critical database that requires an EC2 instance to always be available in a specific AZ. Which option ensures capacity?

exp.a: Incorrect – On-Demand does not guarantee capacity; it may fail during capacity shortages.
exp.b: Incorrect – Spot Instances can be interrupted.
exp.c: Correct – On-Demand Capacity Reservations ensure you have EC2 capacity reserved in a specific AZ when needed.
exp.d: Incorrect – Scheduled Reserved Instances are being deprecated and have limited availability.

q: What is the difference between horizontal scaling and vertical scaling in EC2?

opts.a: Horizontal = adding more instances; Vertical = increasing instance size
opts.b: Horizontal = increasing instance size; Vertical = adding more instances
opts.d: Horizontal = adding more storage; Vertical = adding more memory

exp.a: Correct – Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds more instances. Vertical scaling (scale up) increases the size/power of a single instance.
exp.b: Incorrect – This reverses the definitions.
exp.c: Incorrect – They are different scaling strategies.
exp.d: Incorrect – These are not accurate descriptions.

q: Which AWS service can you use to schedule start/stop of EC2 instances to save costs?

exp.a: Incorrect – AWS Instance Scheduler is one solution but not the only one.
exp.b: Incorrect – EventBridge + Lambda is another valid approach.
exp.c: Correct – Both AWS Instance Scheduler (solution) and EventBridge + Lambda can be used to schedule EC2 start/stop for cost optimization.
exp.d: Incorrect – Trusted Advisor provides recommendations but doesn't schedule instances.

q: What is the maximum number of key pairs you can have per AWS region?

exp.a: Incorrect – The limit is higher than 100.
exp.b: Incorrect – The limit is higher than 500.
exp.c: Correct – You can have up to 5,000 key pairs per AWS region.
exp.d: Incorrect – There is a limit of 5,000.
